row.note: The commentary develops Rab as owner and the flock’s protector; Jacob blesses his descendants through the God who shepherded him all his life, making the personal shepherd relation explicit.
The commentary’s owner and guardian of the herd meets Jacob’s naming of Israel’s God as Shepherd and Rock; the image adds steadfast protection amid Joseph’s affliction.

The commentary’s wild leaders guiding those behind them meets Moses’ request for a leader who goes out and comes in before Israel, lest the congregation be sheep without a shepherd; it connects guidance with accountable rule.
The commentary says Rab is owner and later notes one who names “his Lord”; David calls YHWH “my shepherd,” making ownership a personal relation of trust.
The commentary joins the one who guides a flock to protected pasture; YHWH makes the speaker lie down in green pastures and leads him beside waters, furnishing the same pastoral sequence.
The commentary’s Rab can mean one who sets things right and its guidance image leads the herd; here the shepherd restores the soul and leads in right paths, linking care with moral direction.
The commentary glosses the shepherd as surrounding and protecting livestock; the speaker fears no evil in the dark valley because YHWH is with him and uses rod and staff to comfort him.
The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and evokes a herd; God says every forest animal and cattle on a thousand hills are his, giving the ownership claim concrete scope.

The commentary includes a wild-cattle herd under the r-b-b word family; God says he knows every bird of the mountains and the creatures of the field are his, extending divine ownership to wild creatures.
The commentary’s Rab means owner of everything; God says the world and all it contains are his, grounding the pasture scene in universal possession.
The commentary presents a pasture brought forth for a herd; the psalm depicts pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, adding an image of abundance to divine provision.

The commentary makes the owner, the ones leading ahead, and pasture parts of one scene; God brings Israel out like sheep and leads them through the wilderness, joining divine guidance to flock imagery.
The commentary says the shepherd protects the animals he guides; Israel is led safely here, with the sea overwhelming its enemies, pairing guidance with protection.
The commentary’s owner-guiding-a-flock scene is directly named in the address to the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; the prayer turns the image into a plea for divine attention.
The commentary joins ownership, care, and pasture; the psalm calls worshippers the people of God’s pasture and sheep of his hand, adding belonging to the grazing image.
The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and presents a protected pasture; the psalm says Israel is God’s people and sheep of his pasture, explicitly uniting ownership and flock.
The commentary says the Lord brings forth pasture and that its root-family includes grazing animals; YHWH causes grass to grow for cattle, closely matching divine provision of fodder.
The commentary’s owner produces pasture for dependent herds; all creatures here look to God for food in its season, adding ongoing dependence to the created pasture scene.
The commentary links God’s act of bringing forth pasture with a shepherd’s provision; YHWH covers the sky with clouds and makes grass grow on the mountains, naming the growth as God’s work.
The commentary connects pasture with guarded livestock; God gives animals their food, even young ravens when they cry, extending the provision beyond a human flock.
The commentary’s shepherd surrounds and protects the animals; God gathers lambs in his arms and carries them close, making tender protection part of divine rule.
The commentary says a ruler shepherds and guards his people; Jeremiah condemns shepherds who destroy and scatter God’s pasture-sheep, showing that political care can fail the pastoral duty.
The commentary extends animal care to a ruler’s care of subjects; Jeremiah holds Israel’s shepherds responsible for not attending the flock, sharpening the ethical burden of that analogy.
The commentary’s owner shepherds a flock to its pasture; God promises to gather the remnant from the lands where he scattered them and bring them back, connecting divine ownership with restoration.
The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who protects the herd; the promised shepherds will tend the people so they need not fear or be dismayed, spelling out the result of care.

The commentary says the ruler tends his subjects like a shepherd tends livestock; Ezekiel indicts Israel’s shepherds for feeding themselves rather than the flock, making rule answerable to those cared for.
The commentary defines the shepherd as one who surrounds and protects livestock; Ezekiel’s bad shepherds do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or seek the lost, specifying failures of that care.
The commentary fuses owner and shepherd in one scene; God says he himself will search for and seek his sheep, making divine ownership active rather than merely possessive.
The commentary’s shepherd guards the flock; God rescues his sheep from the cloudy, dark day on which they were scattered, adding rescue at the moment of peril.
The commentary’s owner guides a herd to pasture; God brings the sheep out from the peoples and feeds them on Israel’s mountains, joining gathering, guidance, and grazing.
The commentary calls the pasture protected and supplied; God feeds his sheep in good grazing land and on rich pasture, giving a direct counterpart to the image of pasture provided by its owner.
The commentary’s Lord is the flock’s owner and the shepherd who guards it; God says he will shepherd his sheep and make them lie down, uniting those roles in the same figure.

The commentary’s shepherd protects the herd and watches where affairs will end; God seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak, while judging the fat and strong sheep.

The commentary records Arabic رَعَى (source lexeme in its r-ʿ-y branches) for grazing and tending; Jacob uses Hebrew רעה while offering to pasture Laban’s flock, giving the pastoral sense a specific Semitic lexical counterpart.

row.basis: Grass in the fields for cattle
row.note: The commentary says God brings forth pasture and animals graze it; the promise of rain includes grass in the fields for cattle, making pasture provision part of the land’s gift.
The commentary moves from pasture becoming debris to the temporary life of this world; this psalm compares people to grass swept away, connecting vegetation’s short life to human transience.
The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; the psalm’s grass sprouts in the morning and withers by evening, giving a daily image of swift change.
The commentary reads the pasture’s decay toward the temporary world; human days are compared to grass here, and flourishing to a field flower, carrying the vegetation image into mortality.

row.basis: The place no longer knows it
row.note: The commentary makes the pasture’s transformation a sign of transience; after wind passes over the field-flower, its place knows it no more, sharpening the image of disappearance.
The commentary links pasture turning to debris with the transient worldly life; Isaiah compares all flesh to grass, making human fragility the point of the plant image.
The commentary notes the pasture’s change into waste; Isaiah says grass withers when the breath of YHWH blows on it, adding divine sovereignty over its disappearance.

row.basis: The enduring word contrasts with grass
row.note: The commentary’s pasture decays while its owner knows its end; Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the word of God that stands forever, making permanence the counterpoint to decay.

row.basis: People as sheep without a shepherd
row.note: The commentary extends shepherding from livestock to a ruler’s subjects; Jesus sees the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, making the image a diagnosis of neglected people.
The commentary connects a shepherd’s guidance with care for a community; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins to teach them, showing guidance as an answer to that lack.

row.basis: The shepherd calls his own sheep
row.note: The commentary calls Rab the herd’s owner and describes the one who guides it; the shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining ownership to personal guidance.
The commentary’s leaders among wild animals go ahead and guide the rest; Jesus’ shepherd goes ahead of his sheep and they follow, a close image of leading from the front.
The commentary’s owner guides the herd to pasture; Jesus says those entering through him will go in and out and find pasture, placing access to grazing within the shepherd image.

row.basis: The good shepherd protects the sheep
row.note: The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who surrounds and preserves the animals; Jesus says the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, making protection costly and deliberate.

row.basis: A failed guardian abandons the flock
row.note: The commentary’s shepherd protects livestock; the hired hand sees the wolf, abandons the sheep, and flees, dramatizing the difference between a true guardian and mere employment.
The commentary describes a single owner’s care of a flock; Jesus knows his own sheep and is known by them, adding reciprocal recognition to ownership and tending.
The commentary says the shepherd guards the flock and watches where matters lead; a shepherd searches for one lost sheep until he finds it, showing care as sustained attention to an outcome.

The commentary explicitly says a governor tends his subjects as a shepherd tends livestock; elders are told to shepherd God’s flock and oversee it willingly, applying the pastoral relation to community leadership.
The commentary’s human ruler is a shepherd under the owner’s care; Peter calls Christ the chief Shepherd whose appearing brings a crown, making human oversight subordinate to divine shepherding.
The commentary’s scene brings a flock to pasture under its owner’s guidance; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water, joining shepherding with final provision.

The commentary moves from pasture made waste to the temporary life of this world; Jesus contrasts grass in the field today with its being thrown into the oven tomorrow, using the plant’s short course to teach about trust in God’s provision.
The commentary reads pasture’s decay as a path toward worldly transience; Peter applies Isaiah’s grass-withering image to all flesh and human glory, making mortality explicit.
The commentary presents the Lord as the one who brings forth pasture for herds; creation assigns every beast the green plant for food, placing animal grazing within God’s original provision.

row.basis: Moses as a shepherd before his mission
row.note: The commentary points to Moses’ answer to Pharaoh as its explicit grazing scene; Exodus first shows Moses shepherding Jethro’s flock and bringing it to Horeb, giving that speaker a prior pastoral setting without retelling the Pharaoh encounter.

row.basis: Moses’ compassion for a stray lamb
row.note: The commentary says a shepherd surrounds and protects animals and compares this to a ruler’s care of subjects; this midrash says Moses was chosen after he carried a tired lamb to water, interpreting leadership as attentive care for the vulnerable.

row.basis: A shepherd protects his flock from predators
row.note: The commentary defines the shepherd as protecting livestock; David recounts pursuing a lion or bear that took a lamb from the flock, giving a concrete human example of pastoral guardianship.

row.basis: Rescuing the lamb from the predator
row.note: The commentary’s shepherd preserves the herd; David says he struck the predator and rescued the lamb from its mouth, specifying protection as active recovery.

row.basis: Shepherd and ruler are one role
row.note: The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Israel’s elders tell David that he will shepherd Israel and be its leader, explicitly joining pastoral care and political rule.

row.basis: Moses leads Israel like a flock
row.note: The commentary points to Moses’ pastoral reply to Pharaoh and develops guidance of a herd; the psalm recalls God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, placing the image in the Exodus story.

The commentary links the shepherd of animals to the ruler of people; God takes David from following nursing ewes to shepherd Jacob, making the transition from literal flock care to leadership explicit.
The commentary’s flock leaders guide those behind them and its ruler tends subjects; David shepherds Israel with an upright heart and guides them with skillful hands, uniting care and guidance.

row.basis: Know the state of the flock
row.note: The commentary describes a shepherd who watches where matters will lead and a ruler who tends subjects; this proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flocks and attend to his herds, turning oversight into concrete attention.

row.basis: Stars counted and called by God
row.note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch includes watching the stars and connects oversight with knowing an outcome; Isaiah asks the reader to look at the created host, which God brings out by number and calls by name, relocating cosmic knowledge in the Creator.
The commentary extends shepherding to rulers over people; Isaiah calls Cyrus God’s shepherd, who will carry out the rebuilding of Jerusalem, giving the political metaphor a foreign royal instance.

row.basis: Moses leads God’s flock through the sea
row.note: The commentary invokes Moses speaking of grazing to Pharaoh; Isaiah recalls the one who brought Moses and God’s flock up from the sea, connecting the named speaker with God’s shepherding in the Exodus deliverance.

The commentary says rulers shepherd their subjects and the herd’s leaders guide others; God promises shepherds who will feed the people with knowledge and understanding, specifying instruction as a form of guidance.

The commentary’s herd leaders are those who guide others; Jeremiah describes lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray in the mountains, showing the same leadership relation reversed into misguidance.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and watches over the herd; Ezekiel’s sheep wander across mountains and hills with no one searching for them, portraying the result when pastoral oversight fails.
The commentary pairs a protected pasture with a shepherd who guards it; Ezekiel asks why well-fed sheep trample the rest of the pasture, making care for shared grazing land part of the pastoral duty.
The commentary’s pasture is a provision belonging to the flock; Ezekiel says God’s sheep must eat what the strong sheep have trampled, adding harm within the flock to the image.
The commentary makes the owner, the flock, and its guide parts of one scene; God promises one shepherd, his servant David, over the sheep, linking divine ownership with a human ruler’s care.

The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Micah’s ruler stands and shepherds his flock in YHWH’s strength, after which the people dwell securely, joining leadership, divine backing, and protection.

row.basis: Stars as a sign of future outcome
row.note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch connects watching stars with seeing where an affair will end; God brings Abram outside to look at the stars as a sign of his future descendants, a related but distinct use of the heavens to frame what is to come.

row.basis: Watching stars and refusing their worship
row.note: The commentary mentions star-watching as a secondary r-ʿ-y sense while assigning the ultimate oversight to the Lord; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, and stars, adding a caution about confusing observation with divine rule.

The commentary connects pasture brought forth by God with grazing animals; Isaiah promises rain for seed and fodder for livestock, then says the land’s produce will be rich, joining animal provision to the land’s yield.

The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; Joel depicts cattle groaning and herds wandering because there is no pasture, showing the consequence for dependent animals when grazing land is lost.

row.basis: Peter told to shepherd Jesus’ sheep
row.note: The commentary extends the shepherd’s care to a ruler’s subjects; the risen Jesus tells Peter to shepherd his sheep, transferring pastoral responsibility to a human leader.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and tends livestock; Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep, specifying practical provision as part of the leadership charge.
The commentary says a governor shepherds his subjects; Paul charges overseers to shepherd God’s church, which God acquired, making pastoral leadership both delegated and accountable.

The commentary describes the shepherd as one who watches over and protects a flock; Peter says the addressees returned from straying like sheep to the shepherd and guardian of their souls, applying the image to spiritual oversight.

The commentary compares a ruler’s care for subjects with a shepherd’s care for livestock; Peter tells elders not to dominate those entrusted to them but to be examples, adding an ethical limit to pastoral authority.

row.basis: The great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: The commentary’s Rab is owner and shepherd of the flock; Hebrews calls Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep, grounding pastoral leadership in God’s covenant and the raising of Jesus from the dead.

The commentary says a ruler shepherds his subjects; Revelation depicts the child destined to shepherd all nations with an iron rod, preserving the political shepherd image while giving it a forceful judgment register.
